destination.title: The website he took from never wanted him charged

short23: The website he took from didn't even want him charged.
Aaron Swartz was a programming prodigy.
As a teenager he co-authored the RSS specification and helped build Creative Commons, believing knowledge paid for by the public should belong to the public.
Over MIT's open network, he downloaded about four point eight million scholarly articles — most of the JSTOR archive.
JSTOR settled and said it did not want him prosecuted.
Prosecutors charged him anyway — four counts, then thirteen.

On paper the charges stacked to a theoretical maximum of thirty-five years; but prosecutors signaled a plea of about six months, and legal scholars said that headline wildly overstated what he really faced.
Aaron Swartz died by suicide on January 11, 2013, at age 26.
His family said the prosecution's overreach contributed to his death.
If you're struggling, you can call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: There is a real chance you have never heard it.
Aaron Swartz was born in 1986, just outside Chicago, into a world that was only beginning to come online.
He arrived there through that merger rather than starting the site himself, so the title is genuinely disputed, and honestly, he never seemed to care about it one way or the other.
Because money, for Aaron, was never really the point.
In 2008, he wrote that belief down, in a short and fierce little document he called the Guerilla Open Access Manifesto.
Around 2010, though, his attention started to turn toward something much bigger than any single tool.
The actual rules that govern every one of us, written in a dense language that most ordinary people are never taught to read.
At first, almost nobody outside Washington was paying any attention at all.
On January the 18th, 2012, the internet itself went dark in protest.
It remains, to this day, one of the largest coordinated online protests in human history, and Aaron Swartz was one of its central organizers.
In the autumn of 2010, he carried a laptop onto the campus of MIT, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, one of the most famous universities on earth.
And to this very day, after everything that followed, no one has ever actually proven what he meant to do with all of it.
He never told anyone, and now he never will.
A brilliant young man, alone in a wiring closet, quietly and patiently copying most of a library that he believed should never have been locked in the first place.
In January 2011, Aaron was identified, tracked, and arrested.
The downloading stopped completely and was never resumed.
In July 2011, federal prosecutors charged Aaron Swartz with four felonies, under two separate laws.
Then, a full year later, in September 2012, the prosecutors did something that turned the heat up very sharply indeed.
